To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the maximum attainable gain in single-stage micro-pattern detectors, irradiated with soft X-rays and alpha particles, is limited to 10 5 ; (ii) the gain is increased by at most one order of magnitude when the amplification is shared between two detectors in cascade; and, (iii) a discharge in the first stage is followed by a discharge in the second one, and this is not necessarily a consequence of the first stage operating at a voltage above Raether's

the maximum gain of single-stage gaseous detectors, under irradiation, is limited by Raether's criterion; the maximum gain of multiple-stage gaseous devices is not limited by this criterion; and, the maximum gain of a single device is proportional to the voltage across it, while that of a multiple device is proportional to their total voltage, and thus is larger.
the maximum attainable gain of a gaseous proportional detector is a few 10 ^{5} and that the maximum attainability of such gain is strongly dependent on the detector geometry.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the high-rate performance of micro-pattern detectors, with particular emphasis on the maximum gain that can be achieved in the presence of a large flux of ionizing radiation.
the study of gaseous micro-pattern devices as particle detectors, and in particular with their behavior when operated at high rates and high gain.
the study of the maximum gain that a gaseous detector can achieve when irradiated with X-rays and heavy ionizing particles.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, for a given detector, the maximum achievable rate is inversely proportional to the maximum achievable gain.
the maximum gain of gaseous proportional detectors, when irradiated with soft X-rays and alpha particles, is in the range of 10 5 - 10 6.
micro-pattern gaseous detectors, in their current stage of development, are not suitable for the high-rate environment of the LHC.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the maximum rate capability of a detector is not only a function of its geometry but also of its operating voltage.
the maximum gain of gaseous detectors, in general, is limited to values of 10 5, while for multiple devices, the limit can be pushed up to 10 6, with an acceptable margin for the LHC environment.
, in order to operate safely at high rate, a detector should be designed with a maximum gain below 10 6 and a minimum of two amplifying stages in cascade.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the maximum gain of a single-stage detector is not a reliable indicator of its maximum operating gain in a real experiment.
the maximum gain achievable by gaseous detectors is not limited by the intrinsic properties of the gas, but by the design of the amplification region.

the high rate behavior of gaseous detectors can be reliably predicted from a set of simple and easily reproducible measurements, and that this is the only viable way to assess the performance of detectors for the LHC upgrade.
